source.title_on_document: The hidden costs of AI-assisted ideation: empirical findings on ChatGPT's impact on novice designers' creative confidence and design process

supplement.holds: Concept template (Appendix A) and the full interview script (pp. 11 and 15). The main text prints all test statistics used here (Tables 9 and 10).

paper_design_summary: Thirty-five second-year User Experience Design bachelor students each generated three design concepts without generative AI and then three concepts with ChatGPT 3.5, as homework over two weeks, in a fixed order (no-AI first) that was not randomized. Two expert designers rated the concepts blind to condition on originality, applicability, effectiveness, and clarity, and students self-reported creative confidence, process experience, and perceived novelty and usefulness. Conditions were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

studies.label: Within-subject course-embedded ideation study (no GenAI, then ChatGPT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomly assigned. Every participant did the no-GenAI condition first and the ChatGPT condition second (fixed order). Students were divided across six design briefs by project group.
assignment.quote: We used a fixed order (first no support, followed by ChatGPT use) to avoid contaminating the non-AI baseline with AI-derived prompts and examples.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 4.2 (also Figure 3: 'Fixed order: Condition 1 always preceded Condition 2')

arms.name: Without GenAI
arms.description: Condition 1: three design concepts generated without any generative AI tools

arms.name: With ChatGPT
arms.description: Condition 2: three additional design concepts generated with the support of ChatGPT 3.5

participants.exclusions: Of 96 enrolled students, 63 consented; inclusion required the pre-experiment questionnaire, post-ideation reflection questionnaires for both conditions, all concept templates, and ChatGPT conversation transcripts. The 35 students who completed all required materials formed the final analyzed sample. The paper reports attrition of 44.5%, possibly because submission of research materials was voluntary within a mandatory course activity; baseline measures were unavailable to compare completers and non-completers. One student who mistakenly entered 2024 as year of birth was excluded from age analysis only and retained in the other analyses. These are enrollment, consent, and completion counts, not randomized counts (p. 9, Section 4.1).
participants.who: Second-year bachelor students in a User Experience Design studio course (96 enrolled, 63 consented; the 35 who submitted all questionnaires, concept templates, and ChatGPT transcripts form the sample). Ages 20-29, 77.1 percent female. The same 35 people are in both conditions.
participants.quote: Of the 96 students, 63 provided informed consent to take part in the study. ... Thirty-five students met these criteria and formed the final sample (N = 35).
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 4.1; Tables 9-10 (pp. 21-22) give N = 35 per condition

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT during individual ideation as homework; no constraints on technique; students submitted conversation transcripts (pp. 9-10).

task.description: Individual ideation of design concepts for one of six 'shared space' design briefs (e.g., a meeting place for government, developers, and citizens); each concept documented in a template with a written description and a sketch or image.
task.duration: Two weeks as homework for both conditions combined (p. 10, Figure 3)

eligibility.reason: Two independent failures. Criterion 1: within-subject design with a fixed, non-randomized order (no-GenAI always first, ChatGPT second; p. 10, Section 4.2, Figure 3), so the design is quasi_people, not a randomized experiment. Criterion 2: 35 people analyzed across both conditions (p. 9, Section 4.1; Tables 9-10), well below 50. Criterion 3 is met by blind expert creativity ratings of the concepts (p. 13, Section 4.3.3); self-reported novelty and usefulness do not qualify. Context class set to observational because the form folds quasi_people there; codebook open question 3 may instead keep it in the screening report only. Count note: p. 13 says 214 concepts, 'six per participant', and Table 9 shows 107 concepts per condition, although 35 x 6 = 210; the paper does not explain the difference.

one_line_finding: Among 35 design students who ideated first without AI and then with ChatGPT (fixed order; pp. 9-10, Sections 4.1-4.2), no statistically significant difference in expert-rated creativity was detected (without AI vs with ChatGPT: participant-level medians of students' mean concept scores 3.37 vs 3.29, Z = -0.418, p = .676; idea-level medians 3.25 vs 3.37, Z = -0.281, p = .779; p. 15, Section 4.3.3; pp. 21-22, Tables 9-10), while self-reported confidence, engagement, stimulation, flow, and energy were lower with ChatGPT (pp. 18-21, Sections 5.2.1-5.2.2, Tables 2 and 8).
